SwiftUI Agent Skill for AI Coding Assistants

An agent skill that helps AI coding assistants write smarter, simpler, and more modern SwiftUI, including guidance on API usage, design, performance, and accessibility. Covers navigation, layout, animations, state management, VoiceOver, deprecated API, and more, targeting the mistakes LLMs actually make.

Also available:

SwiftData Pro
Swift Concurrency Pro
Swift Testing Pro

Find more agent skills for Swift and Apple platform development at Swift Agent Skills.

The skill builds upon my existing AGENTS.md file, meaning that you can bring years of knowledge and practical experience into your coding agent of choice in just a few minutes. It uses the Agent Skills format, so it works smoothly with Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, and more.

Installing SwiftUI Pro

If you’re using Xcode, watch the YouTube video on How to Install and Use Agent Skills in Xcode for a walkthrough.

Using SwiftUI Pro

The skill is called SwiftUI Pro, and can be triggered in various ways. For example, in Claude Code you would use this:

/swiftui-pro

And in Codex you would use this:

$swiftui-pro

In both cases you can provide specific instructions if you want only a partial review. For example, /swiftui-pro Check for deprecated API on Claude, or $swiftui-pro Focus on accessibility in Codex.

Use the SwiftUI Pro skill to look for performance problems in this project.

Why Use an Agent Skill for SwiftUI?

This skill is built on thousands of hours of learning, experimenting, and building real-world SwiftUI projects. The rules contained here directly target common SwiftUI mistakes made by LLMs. They sometimes make buttons invisible to VoiceOver, they frequently use deprecated API, and they would often write code that causes surprise performance problems.

You can read more about why I created this skill in my article: SwiftUI Agent Skill - Write better code with Claude, Codex, and other AI tools.

Contributing

I welcome all contributions, whether that's adding new checks, improving existing checks, or editing this README – everyone is welcome!

Keep your Markdown concise. There is a token cost to using skills, particularly with SKILL.md, so please respect the token budgets of users.
Do not repeat things that LLMs already know, because it burns tokens for no benefit. Focus on edge cases, surprises, soft deprecations, and similar.
All work must be licensed under the MIT license so it can benefit the most people.

Please ensure you abide by the Code of Conduct.

README:
Ghidra Software Reverse Engineering Framework
Ghidra is a software reverse engineering (SRE) framework created and maintained by the
[National Security Agency][nsa] Research Directorate. This framework includes a suite of
full-featured, high-end software analysis tools that enable users to analyze compiled code on a
variety of platforms including Windows, macOS, and Linux. Capabilities include disassembly,
assembly, decompilation, graphing, and scripting, along with hundreds of other features. Ghidra
supports a wide variety of processor instruction sets and executable formats and can be run in both
user-interactive and automated modes. Users may also develop their own Ghidra extension components
and/or scripts using Java or Python.

In support of NSA's Cybersecurity mission, Ghidra was built to solve scaling and teaming problems
on complex SRE efforts, and to provide a customizable and extensible SRE research platform. NSA has
applied Ghidra SRE capabilities to a variety of problems that involve analyzing malicious code and
generating deep insights for SRE analysts who seek a better understanding of potential
vulnerabilities in networks and systems.

If you are a U.S. citizen interested in projects like this, to develop Ghidra and other
cybersecurity tools for NSA to help protect our nation and its allies, consider applying for a
[career with us][career].

Security Warning
WARNING:** There are known security vulnerabilities within certain versions of Ghidra. Before
proceeding, please read through Ghidra's [Security Advisories][security] for a better understanding
of how you might be impacted.

Install
To install an official pre-built multi-platform Ghidra release:
Install [JDK 25 64-bit][jdk]
Download a Ghidra [release file][releases]
NOTE:** The official multi-platform release file is named
ghidra_ _ _ .zip which can be found under the "Assets" drop-down.
Downloading either of the files named "Source Code" is not correct for this step.
Extract the Ghidra release file
NOTE:** Do not extract on top of an existing installation
Launch Ghidra: ./ghidraRun (ghidraRun.bat for Windows)
or launch [PyGhidra][pyghidra]: ./support/pyghidraRun (support\pyghidraRun.bat for Windows)

For additional information and troubleshooting tips about installing and running a Ghidra release,
please refer to the [Getting Started][gettingstarted] document which can be found at the root of a
Ghidra installation directory.

Build

To create the latest development build for your platform from this source repository:

Install build tools:
[JDK 25 64-bit][jdk]
[Gradle 9.1.0+][gradle] (or provided Gradle wrapper if Internet connection is available)
[Python3][python3] (version 3.9 to 3.15) with bundled pip
GCC or Clang, and make (Linux/macOS-only)
[Microsoft Visual Studio][vs] 2017+ or [Microsoft C++ Build Tools][vcbuildtools] with the
following components installed (Windows-only):
MSVC
Windows SDK
C++ ATL

Download and extract the source:
[Download from GitHub][master]

NOTE:** Instead of downloading the compressed source, you may instead want to clone the GitHub
repository: git clone https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra.git

Download additional build dependencies into source repository:
NOTE:** If an Internet connection is available and you did not install Gradle, the
./gradlew (or gradlew.bat) command may be used in place of the gradle command in the following
instructions.

Create development build:

The compressed development build will be located at build/dist/.

For more detailed information on building Ghidra, please read the [Developer's Guide][devguide].

For issues building, please check the [Known Issues][known-issues] section for possible solutions.

Develop

User Scripts and Extensions
Ghidra installations support users writing custom scripts and extensions via the *GhidraDev* plugin
for Eclipse. The plugin and its corresponding instructions can be found within a Ghidra release at
Extensions/Eclipse/GhidraDev/ or at [this link][ghidradev]. Alternatively, Visual Studio Code may
be used to edit scripts by clicking the Visual Studio Code icon in the Script Manager.
Fully-featured Visual Studio Code projects can be created from a Ghidra CodeBrowser window at
_Tools -> Create VSCode Module project_.

NOTE:** Both the *GhidraDev* plugin for Eclipse and Visual Studio Code integrations only support
developing against fully built Ghidra installations which can be downloaded from the
[Releases][releases] page.

Advanced Development
To develop the Ghidra tool itself, it is highly recommended to use Eclipse, which the Ghidra
development process has been highly customized for.

Install build and development tools:
Follow the above build instructions so the build completes without errors
Install [Eclipse IDE for Java Developers][eclipse]

Prepare the development environment:

Import Ghidra projects into Eclipse:
File* -> *Import...*
General* | *Existing Projects into Workspace*
Select root directory to be your downloaded or cloned ghidra source repository
Check *Search for nested projects*
Click *Finish*

When Eclipse finishes building the projects, Ghidra can be launched and debugged with the provided
Ghidra** Eclipse *run configuration*.

For more detailed information on developing Ghidra, please read the [Developer's Guide][devguide].

Contribute
If you would like to contribute bug fixes, improvements, and new features back to Ghidra, please
take a look at our [Contributor's Guide][contrib] to see how you can participate in this open
source project.

title: Build self-improving document processing using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: Learn how to build an agentic intelligent document processing (IDP) system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention, automatically handling new document formats without manual template configuration.
content:
IDC research shows that document-related challenges cost organizations $19,732 for each information worker annually and reduce productivity by 21.3 percent. Organizations receiving invoices from hundreds of suppliers often face layouts that vary by issuer and change without notice. Template-based systems require constant maintenance at this scale. Staff can spend up to 30 percent of their time on document-related tasks, and manual data entry error rates range from 1–4 percent . Conventional intelligent document processing (IDP) solutions address some of this burden, but they require extensive upfront configuration for each document format and break when layouts vary across vendors.
In this post, you learn how to build an agentic IDP system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that classifies, extracts, validates, and learns from business documents with minimal human intervention. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Your agents automatically handle new document formats, such as supplier invoices, purchase orders, insurance claims, and loan applications. By the end of this post, you can:

Deploy a multi-agent IDP system, often in under 20 minutes.
Process new document types without manual template configuration.
Let agents train themselves on each new document format and reuse what they learn, so later documents of that type go straight to extraction without retraining.

Challenges with rule-based document processing
Many IDP pipelines require you to define templates, extraction rules, and validation logic for every document format upfront. When a new vendor sends a purchase order with a different layout, the pipeline breaks. This creates three core challenges:

Template rigidity: Each new document format requires manual configuration, and even minor layout changes can cause extraction failures.
No learning: The same extraction errors repeat across similar documents because the system doesn’t retain knowledge from previous corrections.
Scaling burden: Each new vendor or document variant multiplies the maintenance effort, and organizations processing documents from hundreds of sources face ongoing operational costs.

An agentic approach addresses these challenges. Instead of static templates, AI agents analyze each document, generate extraction instructions, validate results, and learn from corrections automatically. Over time, your system builds a knowledge base of document formats, so you process similar documents with minimal additional configuration.
Solution overview
In this solution, eight specialized agents collaborate across two graph-based workflows running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
The following diagram shows the multi-agent workflow graph built using Strands Agents , an open source SDK for building AI agents.

Figure 1: Multi-agent orchestration workflow graph

Identification workflow : The Analyzer agent extracts text using Amazon Textract and identifies the document type and sender. The Matcher agent searches for similar documents using vector similarity in Amazon S3 Vectors , a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3).
Training workflow (new document types): When no match is found, the Instructions agent generates extraction prompts, the Extractor agent extracts structured data, and the Validator agent checks results against schemas and business rules in Amazon Aurora DSQL . If validation fails, the Instructions Fixer agent refines the prompts and retries. On success, the Save Instructions agent persists the instructions for reuse.
Automation workflow (known document types): When a match is found, the Extractor agent uses existing instructions. If validation fails, the Troubleshooter agent fixes the extracted data directly without modifying instructions.

How it works
The following diagram shows the infrastructure architecture for the solution.

Figure 2: Agentic IDP infrastructure architecture on AWS

Business documents arrive in Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) or direct upload to Amazon S3.
Amazon EventBridge triggers an AWS Lambda function that creates a tracking job in Amazon DynamoDB and invokes AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
AgentCore runtime orchestrates document processing through Strands Agents.
Your agents securely access AWS resources through machine-to-machine credentials managed by AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon Cognito .
Your Lambda functions become agent-compatible tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) interface of AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
Agents extract text using Amazon Textract, classify documents using vector embeddings in S3 Vectors, and validate data against business rules in Aurora DSQL.
Agents access enterprise data through MCP servers to validate extracted content against business rules.
You monitor status and troubleshoot issues through a chat-enabled dashboard hosted on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS).
You gain visibility into agent performance through AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and Amazon CloudWatch telemetry.

Deploy the solution
Follow these steps to deploy the solution infrastructure and web UI to your AWS account.
Prerequisites
To deploy this solution, you must have:

An AWS account .
Access to Amazon Bedrock with Amazon Nova and Anthropic (Claude) models enabled. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock .
Access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (Runtime, Gateway, Identity), S3 Vectors, and Amazon Aurora DSQL in a supported Region .
AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) v2 installed.
Docker installed and running (required for building and deploying container images).
Python 3.11+ and Node.js 18+.
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to create S3 buckets, Lambda functions, DynamoDB tables, Cognito user pools, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories, and Amazon ECS services.

Clone the repository and set up the environment:

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/agenticidp-guidance.git
cd agenticidp-guidance

uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -r requirements.txt

cd ui/orchestrator
npm install
cd ../..

Deploy the stacks:

uv run deploy.py --admin-email your-email@example.com

This deploys six AWS CloudFormation stacks: Core (S3, Cognito, DynamoDB), Gateway (Lambda tools, AgentCore Gateway), Aurora (Amazon Aurora DSQL), Agent (AgentCore runtime, containers), UI Orchestrator (API endpoints), and Modern UI (React app on Amazon CloudFront ). Deployment takes approximately 15–20 minutes.

Verify deployment by checking that each stack shows CREATE_COMPLETE in the CloudFormation console.

Process files and review results
After deployment, you receive an email with the CloudFront URL, username, and temporary password.
Process a document

Sign in to the web UI and choose Process Document .
Upload a sample purchase order from infrastructure/sample_data/purchase_orders/training/ .
The document enters the agent workflow:

The Analyzer agent extracts text and identifies the sender and document type.
The Matcher agent searches for similar documents in the vector store.
For a new document type, the training workflow generates extraction instructions, extracts data, validates it, and saves the instructions for future use.
For a known document type, the automation workflow extracts data using existing instructions and validates it.

Review results in the Review Jobs and Instructions tab to verify extracted data, validation results, and generated instructions.

Example: A new document type (training workflow)
Suppose you upload the first purchase order from a new retailer, Two Wheel Store. The Matcher agent searches the vector store, finds no similar document, and routes the job through the training workflow.
The Analyzer agent uses Amazon Textract to extract the raw document text:

# PURCHASE ORDER
FROM: Two Wheel Store
Order #: PO-2026-0102-2584
Date: 2026-01-02

## Items Ordered
AC-021 Advanced Computer Qty: 1 $75.61
Colors: cr4321 @ $75.61
...
SB-004 Folding Classic Qty: 8 $9634.32
Colors: cb8901 I Sizes: S @ $1204.29

TOTAL: $14931.54

The Instructions agent generates extraction prompts from the schema, and the Extractor agent produces structured JSON:

{
"po_number": "PO-2026-0102-2584",
"retailer_name": "Two Wheel Store",
"order_date": "2026-01-02T00:00:00Z",
"line_items": [
{ "sku": "AC-021", "product_name": "Advanced Computer", "quantity": 1, "unit_price": 75.61, "line_total": 75.61 },
{ "sku": "SB-004", "product_name": "Folding Classic", "quantity": 8, "unit_price": 1204.29, "line_total": 9634.32 }
],
"order_total": 14931.54
}

The Validator agent checks the result against the schema and fails :

validation_status: INVALID
error: 'SB-004' does not match '^AB-[A-Z]{2}-\d{3}$'

The vendor’s SKU format ( SB-004 ) doesn’t match Acme Bikes’ internal format ( AB-SB-004 ). The Instructions Fixer agent diagnoses the mismatch and adds an explicit SKU transformation rule to the extraction prompt: prefix vendor SKUs with AB- . On the second pass, the seven line items validate successfully, and the Save Instructions agent persists the refined prompt to the vector store. End-to-end time for this first run: 3 minutes 49 seconds.
Example: A known document type (automation workflow)
When a second purchase order from Two Wheel Store arrives, the Matcher agent finds the stored instructions from the first run with a confidence score of 3.946 (threshold: 3.7) and routes the job through the automation workflow:

The Extractor agent applies the stored instructions directly, so the orchestrator skips prompt generation. The SKU transformation rule learned during training applies automatically ( EL-002 → AB-EL-002 , HB-071 → AB-HB-071 , PD-002 → AB-PD-002 ).
The three line items validate on the first pass with an order total of $5,979.19.
End-to-end processing completes in 1 minute 30 seconds, down from 3 minutes 49 seconds on the first run.

Use the interactive chat
The dashboard includes a chat interface for troubleshooting:

Ask what tools do you have to see available agent capabilities.
Ask list instructions to view stored extraction instructions.
Ask what is the status of job XXXX to check processing progress.
Ask what went wrong with job XXXX, how can we update the instructions? to diagnose failures.

Understand how accuracy improves over time
The system improves over time through two feedback loops:

Training loop : When the Instructions Fixer agent refines extraction prompts after validation failures, the improved instructions are saved and reused for similar documents.
Processing loop : When the Troubleshooter agent fixes extraction errors, it provides detailed analysis that helps identify patterns in document format variations.

When changing models, use AgentCore Evaluations , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to confirm that extraction quality remains acceptable. The solution already uses AgentCore Observability, so it has the required instrumentation.
Estimated cost
You pay only for what you use, because the solution runs on serverless and on-demand resources with no idle costs. For a workload of 10 training documents and 1,000 processed documents each month in US East (N. Virginia), the estimated cost is approximately $58 per month. Foundation model (FM) inference through Amazon Bedrock represents approximately 85 percent of the total cost, at roughly $0.055 per document. Actual cost depends largely on the models assigned to each agent. Model choices are centralized in agents/orchestratorgraph/utils/config.py , so you can use lower-cost models for simpler tasks and stronger models where needed. For detailed pricing, refer to the Amazon Bedrock pricing page.
Customize the solution for your use case
You get a purchase order processing use case with a synthetic bike company dataset, a pre-built JSON schema, and a validation Lambda function that checks extracted data against product and vendor records in a mock ERP database. To process your own documents, you must replace the included schemas and validation logic with your own.
Define your document schema
Create a JSON schema that defines the fields you want to extract for each document type. The sample purchase order schema in agents/orchestratorgraph/doc_schema/purchase_order_schema.json provides a reference. Your schema should specify field names, data types, and whether each field is explicitly stated in the document or inferred from context.
Build your validation process
The included validator checks purchase order data against synthetic vendor and product tables in Aurora DSQL. Your production implementation requires a validation process tailored to your business rules. For example:

An invoice validator might check vendor IDs against your accounts payable system and verify line item totals match the invoice total.
A contract validator might verify that the document contains required clauses and that dates and party names match your records.
A claims validator might check policy numbers, coverage limits, and claimant information against your policy management system.

To add a new validator, create a Lambda function that accepts extracted JSON and returns a pass/fail result with detailed error messages, then register it as a tool in AgentCore Gateway. Refer to gateway/tools/po_validator_tool/ for the implementation pattern.
Update agent prompts
The agent prompts in agents/orchestratorgraph/prompts/ reference purchase order terminology. Update these prompts to reflect your document types and extraction requirements. The Orchestrator agent, Validator agent, and Instructions agent each contain document-type-specific language that you should adapt.
Best practices
Keep these recommendations in mind as you train and operate your agentic IDP system.

Start with representative samples : Upload 5–10 documents per type during training, including edge cases with format variations, to build reliable extraction instructions.
Use business rule validation : Connect validators to your reference data (vendor lists, product catalogs) in Aurora DSQL to catch extraction errors early.
Monitor agent performance : Use AgentCore Observability and CloudWatch to track execution paths, identify bottlenecks, and measure extraction accuracy over time.
Add document types incrementally : Create a JSON schema for each new document type and a corresponding validation Lambda function. The agents handle the rest.
Add guardrails for production : Apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content filtering and grounding checks on agent outputs. This is especially important when you process sensitive document types such as insurance claims or loan applications.
Review the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs : Consult the OWASP Top 10 for LLMs and Generative AI Apps for security considerations when building applications that use large language models (LLMs).

Clean up
Important: Before running cleanup, export the data you want to retain. The destroy.py script permanently deletes processed documents (S3), job history (DynamoDB), validation data (Aurora DSQL), and learned extraction instructions (vector store).
To avoid ongoing charges, remove the deployed resources:

uv run destroy.py

Verify that the six CloudFormation stacks are deleted on the console: AgenticIDP-Core-Dev, AgenticIDP-Gateway-Dev, AgenticIDP-Aurora-Dev, AgenticIDP-Agent-Dev, AgenticIDP-UIOrchestr-Dev, and AgenticIDP-ModernUI-Dev.
Conclusion
In this post, you learned how to build a self-improving document processing system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, where specialized AI agents collaborate to classify, extract, validate, and learn from business documents. This agentic approach adapts to new document formats automatically and improves accuracy over time through feedback loops, replacing manual template configuration with autonomous learning.
As next steps:

Deploy the sample solution and test with the included purchase order samples.
Add your own document types by creating JSON schemas and validation rules.
Explore how to integrate extracted data with downstream systems such as ERP, CRM, or content management tools.

To learn more about the services and patterns used in this post, refer to the following resources:

For a deep dive into the agent framework used in this solution, refer to Strands Agents SDK: A technical deep dive into agent architectures and observability .

For details on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capabilities, refer to the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation .

title: Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
summary: This post walks you through building an AI agent system with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates PowerPoint presentation creation from enterprise documents. A supervisor agent, Retrieval Augmented Generation, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails generate grounded presentations in under 90 seconds.
content:
A financial services team spends significant time each week manually creating client PowerPoint presentations from quarterly reports, compliance documents, and market analyses. Each presentation requires reading hundreds of pages, extracting key data points, structuring slides, and generating supporting visuals. This post walks you through building an AI agent system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates this workflow, completing in under 90 seconds in our internal testing. This approach reduces presentation creation time while grounding content in source documents. The solution deploys a supervisor agent on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using the Strands Agents framework to orchestrate document generation and summarization tools. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (available on Amazon Bedrock) handles content creation, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 powers vector search, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available on Amazon Bedrock) generates slide images. This post includes a public repository with the code assets.
Solution overview
The solution deploys a single supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime that selects between document generation and summarization tools based on user requests. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline uses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector storage and semantic search across multimodal content.
The solution includes a REST API built with .NET 8 minimal APIs, so you can integrate with existing enterprise applications through standard HTTP calls. AWS Lambda offers serverless compute, including containerized functions for PowerPoint generation. The solution secures the implementation with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) isolation, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) least-privilege access control.
Key concepts
This section covers AgentCore runtime, RAG, and content safety guardrails as they apply to this solution.
Agent orchestration with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
A single AI agent generating documents from large knowledge bases must retrieve content, structure outlines, generate text, create images, and assemble files. Rather than implementing these competing responsibilities in a monolithic function, the solution uses a tool-based architecture where a supervisor agent routes requests to specialized tools.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent code runs in an isolated container with session management, built-in identity, and observability. The solution uses the Strands Agents framework (an open source SDK for building AI agents) to implement the supervisor logic.
The supervisor agent exposes two tools:

generate_pptx: Creates PowerPoint presentations by invoking the PPTX Generator Lambda function, which retrieves content from the knowledge base, generates slide outlines, creates AI images, and assembles the final document.
generate_summary: Extracts and synthesizes information from the knowledge base using RAG to deliver accurate, grounded responses.

The agent determines whether a request requires document generation, content summarization, or both, then invokes the appropriate tool. You can add new capabilities by defining new tools in the agent code without modifying existing ones.
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) for enterprise knowledge
RAG addresses a fundamental challenge in AI systems: delivering accurate, up-to-date information grounded in enterprise data rather than relying solely on the model’s training data. The implementation uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , which combine vector search with large language models (LLMs) to retrieve relevant context before generating responses.
The RAG pipeline works as follows:

You upload enterprise documents to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) .
The system chunks and parses documents, applying special handling for multimodal content including tables, charts, and images.
Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 converts each chunk into high-dimensional vectors that capture semantic meaning.
Amazon OpenSearch Serverless stores the vectors, creating a searchable vector database.
At query time, the system converts the user’s request into an embedding and performs similarity search to retrieve relevant document chunks.
Retrieved chunks supply context to the language model, which generates responses grounded in the source material.

This approach is designed to help reduce hallucinated content by grounding generated documents in source information from the enterprise knowledge base.
Note: The Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection data plane must remain publicly accessible because Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases accesses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless from AWS-managed infrastructure, not through customer VPC endpoints. IAM data access policies protect the collection, and VPC-only access restricts the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless dashboard.
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content safety
Enterprise AI applications require content moderation to meet organizational standards and compliance requirements. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offers built-in content filtering and safety mechanisms integrated throughout the document generation pipeline.
Guardrails operate at multiple stages:

Input processing: Filters user requests to help prevent injection issues and inappropriate content.
Output generation: Monitors model outputs to verify compliance with content policies.
Personally identifiable information (PII) handling: Detects and anonymizes or blocks PII.

The implementation creates custom guardrails through AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) , configured with specific policies tailored to enterprise document creation. The agent applies guardrails at the model invocation level, providing consistent content safety without requiring manual configuration for each deployment.
Solution architecture
The following diagram illustrates the agent-based document generation system.

Figure 1: Architecture of the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore RAG presentation generation system

The data flow begins with user requests arriving through Amazon API Gateway , which routes them to a .NET-based Chat API running on AWS Lambda . The API maintains conversation state in Amazon DynamoDB . It then invokes the supervisor agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime.
The supervisor agent analyzes the request and selects the appropriate tool. For document generation, it invokes the PPTX Generator Lambda (a containerized Python function). For summarization, the supervisor invokes the Summary Generator Lambda, which queries the knowledge base through the retrieve_and_generate API.
The system processes, chunks, and embeds documents stored in Amazon S3 using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless indexes the embeddings for fast semantic search. When tools query the knowledge base, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless retrieves relevant chunks, which are then supplied as context to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (on Amazon Bedrock) for generating grounded responses.
The system stores generated documents in Amazon S3 and returns presigned URLs for secure download. Security measures include:

AWS WAF with managed rule sets and IP-based rate limiting on Amazon API Gateway.
Amazon Cognito with the Plus feature plan and advanced security mode for threat protection.
Amazon Bedrock Guardrails provisioned through AWS CDK for consistent content filtering.
Amazon DynamoDB with point-in-time recovery, deletion protection, and customer-managed AWS KMS encryption.
Amazon S3 buckets with versioning, server access logging, and block public access.
AWS X-Ray tracing on Lambda functions for distributed debugging.
Input validation with regex-based tenant ID and session ID verification.
Tenant isolation through AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) role assumption per tenant.

Prerequisites
Before deploying, you need the following tools and access configured in your environment:

AWS environment:

An active AWS account with permissions for deploying infrastructure.
AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) configured with credentials.
IAM role with appropriate service access policies.

Development tools:

.NET SDK 8 with Amazon.Lambda.Tools installed globally.
Python 3.12 or later for AWS CDK and Lambda functions.
Node.js and AWS CDK CLI for infrastructure deployment.
Docker or Finch for building container images (ARM64 support required).

AWS services access:

Amazon Bedrock with model access for Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available through Amazon Bedrock). For model availability by Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock .
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore access enabled in your account.
Amazon API Gateway Regional REST API integration timeout configured to at least 300 seconds. The default is 29 seconds. For more information, see API Gateway quotas .
An existing Amazon VPC with private subnets.
An Amazon S3 bucket for deployment artifacts.

Set up the solution
The setup process includes configuring deployment parameters and initializing the AWS CDK environment.

Clone the repository and navigate to the project directory:

git clone https://github.com/aws-samples/sample-generating-powerpoint-presentations-with-amazon-bedrock.git

Create the configuration file pipeline-params.ini at the repository root:

environment=dev
awscliprofile=
ContainerRegistry=lambda-pptx-gen
AgentContainerRegistry=agentcore-supervisor
BucketDev=<amzn-s3-demo-bucket>
VpcId=<your-vpc-id>
ParsingInferenceProfileId=us.anthropic.claude-haiku-4-5-20251001-v1:0
AgentInferenceProfileId=us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6
EmbeddingModelId=amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0
ImageGenerationModelId=stability.stable-image-inpaint-v1:0
PPTXGenImageTag=latest
AgentImageTag=latest

Set awscliprofile to your AWS CLI profile name, or leave empty to use environment variable credentials.
Bootstrap AWS CDK (one-time per account and Region):

cdk bootstrap

This creates the AWS CloudFormation CDKToolkit stack required for AWS CDK deployments.
Make build scripts executable:

chmod +x ./pipeline-build.sh
chmod +x ./pipeline-deploy.sh
chmod +x ./deploy-agentcore.sh

Build and deploy
The deployment consists of three phases: building artifacts, deploying infrastructure, and deploying the AgentCore runtime agent.
Build phase
The build phase compiles application code and packages deployment artifacts. Run the build script:

./pipeline-build.sh

This compiles the .NET projects (Chat API) and packages them as Lambda deployment packages. It builds the PPTX Generator container image using Docker or Finch and authenticates with Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) . It then pushes the container image and stores build artifacts in the asset-output directory.
Infrastructure deployment phase
The infrastructure deployment creates AWS resources and configures service integrations. Run the deployment script:

./pipeline-deploy.sh

The deployment creates four AWS CloudFormation stacks in dependency order:

VPCEndpointsStack: Configures Amazon VPC endpoints for AWS services including Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
OpensearchStack: Provisions Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection for vector storage.
AgentCoreStack: Creates guardrails, Lambda functions, IAM roles, and stores configuration in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store .
ChatApiStack: Deploys Amazon API Gateway and Chat API Lambda.

AgentCore runtime deployment
After the infrastructure stacks are deployed, deploy the supervisor agent to AgentCore runtime:

./deploy-agentcore.sh

This script builds the supervisor agent container (ARM64), pushes it to Amazon ECR, creates the AgentCore runtime and endpoint, and updates the Systems Manager parameter with the endpoint Amazon Resource Name (ARN). The Chat API references this endpoint ARN to route requests to the agent.
After deployment, AWS CloudFormation outputs include the Amazon API Gateway endpoint URL and resource identifiers.
Configuration
The solution offers several configuration points:
Agent instructions
Edit agent/app.py to modify the supervisor agent’s system prompt and behavior. The agent uses Strands Agents with two tools defined in agent/tools.py :

generate_pptx: Invokes the PPTX Generator Lambda for document creation.
generate_summary: Invokes the Summary Generator Lambda for knowledge base queries.

Model selection
In pipeline-params.ini , adjust model identifiers:

ParsingInferenceProfileId : Model for knowledge base document parsing (Anthropic Claude Haiku 4.5 recommended for cost efficiency).
AgentInferenceProfileId : Model for agent reasoning (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 recommended).
EmbeddingModelId : Embedding model for vector search (Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2).
ImageGenerationModelId : Model for slide image generation (Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint).

With inference profiles instead of direct model IDs, requests draw on a broader multi-Region capacity pool, which increases throughput and helps maintain consistent performance under load.
Lambda configuration
Adjust compute resources in the stack files:

Chat API: 128 MB memory, 29-second timeout, 100 reserved concurrency (in api.py ).
PPTX Generator: 900 MB memory, 300-second timeout, 50 reserved concurrency (in pptx_gen.py ).
Summary Generator: 512 MB memory, 300-second timeout, 50 reserved concurrency (in sum_gen.py ).

Results
In internal testing with a 90-page Amazon 2024 Annual Report PDF, the solution produced the following performance metrics:

Presentation generation time: 70–90 seconds end-to-end (including knowledge base retrieval, content generation, image creation, and file assembly).
Slide count: Six slides with title, bullet points, image+text, image-only, and takeaway formats.
Image generation: Two AI-generated images per presentation using Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint.
Cost per generation: Approximately $0.04 in model invocation costs at time of writing in us-east-1 (text and image generation, with image generation accounting for the majority of cost).
Knowledge base ingestion: Under 2 minutes for a single 1.3 MB PDF document.

PowerPoint presentations
The following figures show example slides from a generated presentation.

Figure 2: Generated title slide with customizable branding

Figure 3: Generated content slide with bullet points

Figure 4: Generated slide combining text with an AI-generated image

Figure 5: Generated content slide summarizing profitability metrics

Figure 6: Generated image-only slide with an AI-generated visual

Figure 7: Generated takeaways slide

Generated presentations include:

Title slides with customizable branding.
Content slides with bullet points and structured text.
Image slides with AI-generated visuals from Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (on Amazon Bedrock).
Speaker notes with presentation guidance.
Consistent formatting based on corporate templates.

Summaries
Summary outputs provided to the knowledge base include:

Concise synthesis of knowledge base content.
Citation tracking to source documents.
Structured formatting with key points highlighted.

API responses
The Chat API returns:

Streaming responses for real-time user feedback. Because internal testing showed that presentation generation takes 70–90 seconds (exceeding the default Amazon API Gateway 29-second integration timeout), the Chat API uses an asynchronous invocation pattern. Use streaming or polling to receive the final result rather than waiting on a synchronous REST call.
Conversation context maintenance across multiple turns.
Amazon S3 presigned URLs for document downloads (5-minute expiration).

Generated content undergoes Amazon Bedrock Guardrails validation to verify compliance with content policies before delivery.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the deployed resources:

Delete the AgentCore runtime and endpoint:

aws bedrock-agentcore-control delete-agent-runtime-endpoint \
--agent-runtime-id <runtime-id> \
--agent-runtime-endpoint-id <endpoint-id>

aws bedrock-agentcore-control delete-agent-runtime \
--agent-runtime-id <runtime-id>

Turn off Amazon DynamoDB deletion protection (required before stack deletion):

aws dynamodb update-table --table-name chat-sessions-dev --no-deletion-protection-enabled
aws dynamodb update-table --table-name tenant-table-dev --no-deletion-protection-enabled

Delete AWS CloudFormation stacks in reverse dependency order:

aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name ChatApiStack
aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name AgentCoreStack
aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name OpensearchStack
aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name VPCEndpointsStack

Empty Amazon S3 buckets before deletion (AWS CloudFormation cannot delete non-empty buckets):

aws s3 rm s3://amzn-s3-demo-bucket --recursive

Delete Amazon ECR repositories containing container images:

aws ecr delete-repository --repository-name lambda-pptx-gen --force
aws ecr delete-repository --repository-name agentcore-supervisor --force

Delete tenant knowledge base sub-stacks (created by the tenant provisioner):

aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name bedrock-kb-<tenant-id>

Security considerations
This solution uses Lambda environment variables for configuration values such as model IDs, Amazon S3 bucket names, and guardrail IDs. These are resource identifiers, not secrets. For production deployments, use AWS Secrets Manager for sensitive configuration values such as API keys and database credentials.
The AgentCore runtime agent runs in an isolated container with session-level isolation. Each user session operates in a dedicated environment, helping to prevent cross-session data contamination.
Conclusion
In this post, you built an AI agent system with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates enterprise document generation. The supervisor agent deployed on AgentCore runtime routes requests to specialized tools for document creation and summarization, reducing presentation creation to about 90 seconds in an internal test.
The RAG pipeline grounds generated content in source documents, and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails verifies content compliance. You can adapt this architecture for automated report generation in financial services, technical documentation for engineering teams, or proposal creation for sales organizations.
To get started, clone the GitHub repository and follow the setup instructions. For more information about the services used, refer to the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation , Strands Agents SDK , and AWS CDK Developer Guide .

title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
summary: Learn how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock that autonomously investigates and safely remediates cloud security findings from CNAPP and cloud-native sources. The approach drove a 90%+ reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues.
content:
Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount.
In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues.
About Tamnoon
Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers.
Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale.
Cloud security remediation challenges
A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts.

Alert volume overwhelms headcount: CNAPPs and scanners generate thousands of findings. Teams can’t triage them all, so critical exposures sit unresolved while risk compounds for months.
Investigation is manual and repetitive: Each finding requires context gathering on who owns the resource, what depends on it, whether the fix is safe. This eats hours of senior engineer time, repeated across every item in the backlog.
Fear of production impact blocks automation: Teams hesitate to automate remediation because they can’t risk taking down production. Without confidence that a fix is safe, nothing moves.
Reactive prioritization: Without a way to cluster related findings or score remediation confidence, teams work through alerts linearly rather than addressing root causes that resolve many issues at once.

Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems.
Solution overview
Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely.
Agentic architecture on Amazon Bedrock
The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline:

An investigation agent draws on training from millions of real customer cloud environments to determine context, filters that context through a large language model (LLM)-as-a-judge validation layer. It reasons through the remediation goal, operational scope, and cloud-provider-specific verification, producing read-only investigation steps and a complete investigation plan.
A safety-scoring agent builds an evidence chain per asset, combining automated verification results with analyst findings. It classifies each finding’s remediation as SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA with a deliberately conservative bias. When in doubt, it downgrades.
A remediation agent activates only for findings that the safety agent has deemed safe. It reasons through ordering, dependencies, and conditions, then produces a remediation plan in which every step follows a backup, remediate, and verify structure and includes rollback guidance.
A code-generation agent turns plan steps into executable remediation, but only after an input guardrail screens for relevance and prompt injection. Every artifact passes an automated generate-and-review loop in which a separate reviewer agent must approve the output.

Why Amazon Bedrock
When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement.
That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time.
Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate.
Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to.
How Tamnoon integrates with CNAPPs and cloud security tools
Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows.
For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first.

Figure 1: Tamnoon in action

Tamnoon AWS architecture
Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet.
Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) runs the always-on services behind the dashboard, while AWS Lambda powers the event-driven work of collecting findings, analyzing them, and executing remediations. A set of AWS messaging and workflow services, including Amazon EventBridge, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), and AWS Step Functions, coordinate these steps so large volumes of findings are processed reliably and in parallel, with no single bad record stalling the rest.
The AI layer runs on Amazon Bedrock. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model, gives Tamnoon’s agents a governed way to take action instead of open-ended access. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails then review both the request and the generated code before anything moves forward. Supporting services handle the rest of the platform: managed databases and caching for state, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) for playbooks and artifacts, and AWS Secrets Manager for credentials, so sensitive keys never live in application code.
On the customer side, everything to the left of the AWS Cloud boundary is what customers connect into Tamnoon. They can link their own AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud accounts, plug in the security tools their findings come from, and connect the destinations where they want outcomes delivered, such as Slack, Jira, ServiceNow, and GitHub.

Figure 2: Tamnoon AWS architecture

How Tamnoon maintains zero production issues
Zero production issues is a reality for Tamnoon’s customers, and it is no accident. Autonomy at Tamnoon sits inside a defense-in-depth safety architecture, where each layer assumes the one before it might miss something.
It starts before any fix is even drafted. No remediation is written until an independent safety assessment, focused on scope and deliberately biased toward caution, concludes that the change is safe to make. From there, the platform draws a hard line between reading and writing. Investigation steps are validated as strictly read-only, so the work of understanding a problem can never alter it. Only the remediation path is allowed to change anything, and every change it makes carries its own backup, verification, and rollback steps.
That discipline is reinforced by constant self-critique. Each generation step is paired with a reflection step that checks the output and feeds its critique back into regeneration, so the system is always reviewing its own work rather than trusting it outright. Those recommendations are also kept grounded in reality. Agent output is validated against automation results, user feedback, and training data drawn from real fixed alerts, and when the model cannot reach an accurate result on its own, a human is brought into the loop.
The final safeguard is at the moment of execution. The AI never holds cloud credentials. Instead, execution is brokered through short-lived, tenant-scoped credentials under customer-controlled trust, running in an isolated environment kept separate from the agents that plan the work. Wrapping all of this is human governance: remediations flow through an approval workflow with a full audit trail, and every AI capability is proven internally before it ever reaches a customer.
Data security and compliance
Tami reasons over sensitive customer data: alert payloads, resource identifiers, misconfigurations, and remediation context. That data must stay inside the AWS trust boundary, run with least privilege, and stay auditable. Standardizing on Amazon Bedrock makes that possible.
Sensitive content stays inside AWS
Every Tami workload invokes Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock through the ChatBedrockConverse interface, rather than calling a third-party LLM endpoint. That single choice puts the full AI supply chain under one AWS native service, which has real consequences for how customer data is handled. Inference runs entirely within Tamnoon’s own AWS account in US commercial Regions, so data never leaves AWS. For information about model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . Because Bedrock doesn’t retain or train on prompts or completions, customer data never reaches an external vendor in the first place.
That boundary holds even as workloads scale. Bedrock Cross-Region inference automatically routes requests to Regions within the US geographic boundary, increasing the throughput available to the application. The compute behind it stays private as well. Each service runs as an AWS Lambda function attached to a virtual private cloud (VPC), in private subnets with an explicit security group, no public ingress, and tightly controlled egress.
Guarding what reaches the model
Payloads can carry sensitive detail, so Tami applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to every request and response. The policy is enforced at the Bedrock layer, which means it covers all three services uniformly and no individual function’s prompt logic can bypass it. That single enforcement point does several things at once.
First, it protects sensitive data. PII and secret-like content is masked before it is ever persisted or surfaced, so nothing sensitive lingers where it doesn’t belong. It also guards against prompt injection, which matters because Tami reasons over untrusted findings that an unauthorized user could influence. Filtering at the guardrail layer stops a crafted payload from hijacking the model or exfiltrating context. Finally, denied topics and content filters keep the model’s output scoped to security remediation and nothing else. Every intervention is logged alongside AWS CloudTrail, giving enterprise customers a clear trail of governance evidence.
Least-privilege access
Access across the platform runs through a dedicated per-service IAM execution role, so each function can reach only what it needs and nothing more. That principle is easiest to see in how Tami touches Amazon Bedrock. Its only Bedrock permission is bedrock:InvokeModel , scoped to specific inference-profile and foundation-model ARNs. It has no ability to manage, train, or export models.
The same discipline extends to every other dependency. Access to AWS Secrets Manager is limited to the two secrets a function actually uses, SQS access is confined to its own input queue, and Amazon CloudWatch writes are restricted by namespace. There are no broad, catch-all roles anywhere in the design. Functions attach only to the managed AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole and AWSLambdaVPCAccessExecutionRole policies, and nothing wider than that.
Multi-tenant isolation and governance
Keeping tenants separated is a foundational requirement, and it is enforced from the very first call. Service-to-service calls use OAuth2 client credentials through Cognito, scoped per application, and work is processed one SQS message at a time with its tenant context attached. As a result, a single invocation only ever touches one tenant’s data.
Much of this assurance comes from treating the entire platform as code. IAM policies, network placement, model IDs, and alarms all live in versioned AWS CloudFormation and SAM templates, so every permission and model version is reviewable in source control with no manual console changes to drift out of sync. Model versions in particular are pinned to dated identifiers, for example claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 , which means a model change is always an explicit, reviewed code change rather than a silent upgrade.
That transparency carries through to runtime. Every inference call lands in AWS CloudTrail, attributable to the invoking role, and deterministic decoding with temperature set to zero keeps scoring and planning consistent from one run to the next. Failure handling is governed with the same rigor. Each service has an input queue with redrive, an error-handler function, a dead-letter queue, and CloudWatch alarms on timeouts and DLQ depth wired to on-call. Failures are contained and observable, and never silently dropped.
Results and impact
Tami has analyzed more than 14 million cloud alerts across Tamnoon’s customer base, a number tracked in Tamnoon’s 2026 State of Cloud Remediation report . The decisions Tami makes reflect patterns learned from these real-world environments.
For a typical customer, the results show up fast, usually within 90 days.

Metric
Before
After

Critical cloud exposure
Compounds for months as alerts outpace headcount
Up to 90% reduction in 90 days ( source )

Remediation efficiency
Thousands of raw alerts, no clear prioritization
Up to 100x efficiency through root-cause clustering ( source )

Production issues
Teams avoid automation because of risk
Zero production issues across millions of workloads

Engineer time
Hours per finding, repeated across backlog
13,000+ hours saved per week across customer base ( source )

The compression and zero-issue figures come from Tamnoon’s research. The pattern is consistent, showing fewer open exposures, far less manual work, and no downtime from the fixes themselves.
Conclusion
Building an agent that can reason about a cloud finding is the straightforward part. Building one you’d trust to act on production is the hard part. Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that provides access to high-performing foundation models along with the tooling to build agentic applications: orchestration, tool use, and guardrails, through a single API. That combination matters here for a specific reason: acting on production cloud infrastructure demands both strong reasoning and hard safety boundaries.
Four things make that possible:

title: Deploy and evaluate models with Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
summary: Learn how to deploy an available model from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, run a lightweight and repeatable performance test using the SageMaker Python SDK, and delete the endpoint when testing is complete.
content:
Choosing the right model for a specific application requires a practical way to test it with representative inputs. Amazon SageMaker JumpStart provides access to a broad catalog of already pretrained models. In this post, we show how to deploy an available model from SageMaker JumpStart, run a lightweight and repeatable performance test using the SageMaker Python SDK, and delete the endpoint when testing is complete. For supported models and available capacity, this workflow provides a repeatable evaluation path, although deployment time varies by model, instance type, quota, and AWS Region.
In 2026, SageMaker JumpStart introduced two improvements that simplify model discovery and deployment. In the Model Hub section of the Amazon SageMaker AI console, you can browse the SageMaker JumpStart catalog, view sample notebooks, and open them directly in SageMaker Studio. Pre-configured endpoint deployment options provide named configurations optimized for priorities such as low cost, low latency, or general-purpose workloads across a range of generative AI models, including Neuron-optimized configurations. Additionally, you can now go from Hugging Face model discovery to SageMaker AI deployment in a single click using the new deep link integration.
Solution overview
Our approach uses a reusable Python script that performs three steps:

Discover and deploy a model from SageMaker JumpStart.
Run model-specific sample prompts and measure latency, approximate output length, and single-request generation rate.
Clean up the endpoint.

This pattern works for many compatible SageMaker JumpStart models, although payload formats, required instance types, end-user license agreement (EULA) requirements, and response schemas may require model-specific adjustments.
Prerequisites

An AWS account with SageMaker AI permissions.
Python 3+ with SageMaker Python SDK v3 installed ( pip install "sagemaker>=3,<4" ).
Sufficient GPU instance quota for the model you want to test or request a quota increase .

Step 1.a: Discover available models
UI path to find models in SageMaker JumpStart:

Figure 1: Browsing the model catalog on the SageMaker JumpStart Models page in SageMaker Studio

Code path using SageMaker Python SDK:

from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.notebook_utils import (
list_jumpstart_models,
)

REGION = "us-east-1"

models = list_jumpstart_models(
filter="task == textgeneration",
region=REGION,
list_versions=True,
)

print(f"Found {len(models)} text generation models")

for model_id, model_version in models[:10]:
print(
f" - {model_id} "
f"(version {model_version})"
)

Or search by model name:

from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.notebook_utils import list_jumpstart_models

ids = list_jumpstart_models(
filter="model_id contains qwen",
region=REGION,
list_versions=True,
)

print(f"{len(ids)} models matched in {REGION}\n")

for model_id, version in ids:
print(f"{model_id:<55} v{version}")

Step 1.b: Deploy the model
UI path to deploy models from SageMaker JumpStart:

Figure 2: Deploying a model from its SageMaker JumpStart detail page in SageMaker Studio

Code path using SageMaker Python SDK:

import time

from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.accessors import JumpStartModelsAccessor
from sagemaker.core.jumpstart.configs import JumpStartConfig
from sagemaker.core.training.configs import Compute
from sagemaker.serve import ModelBuilder

MODEL_ID = "huggingface-vlm-qwen3-5-27b"
MODEL_VERSION = "1.13.0"
REGION = "us-east-1"
ACCEPT_EULA = False # Set True only after reviewing the model terms

def get_field(value, name, default=None):
if isinstance(value, dict):
return value.get(name, default)
return getattr(value, name, default)

# Resolve the JumpStart-recommended deployment configuration.
specs = JumpStartModelsAccessor().get_model_specs(
region=REGION,
model_id=MODEL_ID,
version=MODEL_VERSION,
)

if isinstance(specs, list):
if not specs:
raise ValueError(
f"No JumpStart specification found for {MODEL_ID}"
)
specs = specs[0]

recommended_instance_type = get_field(
specs,
"default_inference_instance_type",
)

if not recommended_instance_type:
raise ValueError(
f"No recommended instance type found for {MODEL_ID}"
)

print(f"Model: {MODEL_ID}")
print(f"Region: {REGION}")
print(f"Recommended instance: {recommended_instance_type}")

start = time.time()

jumpstart_config = JumpStartConfig(
model_id=MODEL_ID,
model_version=MODEL_VERSION,
accept_eula=ACCEPT_EULA,
)

model_builder = ModelBuilder.from_jumpstart_config(
jumpstart_config=jumpstart_config,
compute=Compute(
instance_type=recommended_instance_type,
instance_count=1,
),
)

model = model_builder.build()
endpoint = model_builder.deploy()
deploy_time = time.time() - start

print(f"Deployed in {deploy_time:.1f} seconds")
print(f"Endpoint: {endpoint.endpoint_name}")

Step 2: Run sample prompts and measure performance

from sagemaker.core.payloads import retrieve_all_examples
import json
import time

MODEL_ID = "huggingface-vlm-qwen3-5-27b"
MODEL_VERSION = "1.13.0"
REGION = "us-east-1"

example_payloads = retrieve_all_examples(
region=REGION,
model_id=MODEL_ID,
model_version=MODEL_VERSION,
serialize=True,
)

#you can re-create the endpoint pointer using the endpoint name:
#from sagemaker.core.resources import Endpoint
#endpoint = Endpoint.get(endpoint_name="<your_endpoint_name>",region=REGION)

def read_response_body(result):
body = result.body
if hasattr(body, "read"):
body = body.read()
if isinstance(body, bytes):
body = body.decode("utf-8")
if isinstance(body, str):
try:
return json.loads(body)
except json.JSONDecodeError:
return body
return body

def extract_output(response):
"""Handle common JumpStart text-generation response formats."""
if isinstance(response, list):
response = response[0] if response else ""
if isinstance(response, dict):
choices = response.get("choices")
if choices:
choice = choices[0]
message = choice.get("message")
if isinstance(message, dict):
return message.get("content", "")
return choice.get("text", "")
for field in (
"generated_text",
"output_text",
"text",
):
if field in response:
return response[field]
return response

results = []

for payload in example_payloads or []:
start = time.perf_counter()
result = endpoint.invoke(
body=payload.body,
content_type=payload.content_type,
accept=payload.accept,
)
latency = time.perf_counter() - start
response = read_response_body(result)
output = extract_output(response)
if not isinstance(output, str):
output = json.dumps(output, indent=2)
# This is an estimate based on whitespace-separated words.
output_words = len(output.split())
results.append(
{
"request_preview": payload.body[:50],
"latency_s": round(latency, 2),
"estimated_output_words": output_words,
"words_per_second": round(
output_words / latency,
1,
) if latency > 0 else 0,
}
)
print("Input:\n", payload.body, end="\n\n")
print("Output:\n", output, end="\n\n")
print(
f"Latency: {latency:.2f} seconds\n"
f"Estimated output words: {output_words}\n"
f"Estimated single-request output generation rate: "
f"{output_words / latency:.1f} words/second\n"
)
print("-" * 80)

print("\nSummary:")
for result in results:
print(result)

Result:

Input:
{"max_tokens": 256, "messages": [{"content": "What is deep learning?", "role": "user"}], "model": "/opt/ml/model"}
Output:
Here's a thinking process that leads to the explanation of deep learning:
1. **Deconstruct the Request:**
* **Question:** "What is deep learning?"
* **Intent:** The user wants a clear, comprehensive, yet accessible definition and overview of deep learning.
* **Target Audience:** Likely someone looking for a general understanding, possibly a student, tech
enthusiast, or professional exploring the field. The tone should be informative, structured, and
not overly jargon-heavy (though key terms need explanation).
2. **Initial Brainstorming & Key Concepts:**
* What is it? A subset of machine learning, which is a subset of AI.
* Core mechanism: Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs).
* "Deep" means many layers (hidden layers).
* How does it work? Learning representations from data (feature learning).
* Key applications: Image recognition, NLP, speech, self-driving cars.
* Why is it popular now? Big data, GPU power, better algorithms.
* Pros/Cons: High accuracy vs. black box, data hunger.
3. **Structuring the Answer:**
Latency: 9.07 seconds
Estimated output words: 153
Estimated single-request output generation rate: 16.9 words/second
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Summary:
{'request_preview': '{"max_tokens": 256, "messages": {"content": "What', 'latency_s': 9.07, 'estimated_output_words': 153, 'words_per_second': 16.9}

Step 3: Cleanup

print(f"Deleting endpoint: {endpoint.endpoint_name}")
endpoint.delete()
endpoint.wait_for_delete()
print("Endpoint deleted")

Conclusion
This pattern works for many available SageMaker JumpStart models, but the payload format, required instance type, EULA, and response parsing may require model-specific adjustments. By using consistent test prompts and measuring latency, throughput, and output quality across models, you can compare options and select the right fit for your workload.
Try this approach with different models from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart to find the right balance of quality, speed, and cost for your applications.
